newsSourceFindings.finding: The selected workshop series is current as of 16 November 2026. Official pages support the October–November workshop schedule, free participation, team size, registration deadline and February 2027 final. The manuscript distinguishes future hackathon/screening plans from completed events; the timing match is stronger than R10.

The manuscript says the first hackathon ran 1–26 February 2026. That range is the call-for-applications page header; the page body schedules workshops in March and the hackathon on 28–29 March. Do not present the application-page range as the actual hackathon duration.

The figures 1,100 attendees, about 1,300 submissions, 55 selected projects and 12 awards match AMC’s retrospective account and are explicitly attributed to the organizer. This is not independent attendance verification.

The reviewer calls the AIFH 2027 label uncorroborated. The official second-edition AMC page expressly uses that label, including the original retained fetch. Omitting it is harmless, but the review criticism is factually wrong.

Publication instructions and final synthesis claim every requested correction was applied. The final main article still presents the broad industry-transformation sentence and institutional-strategy characterization as factual prose. The LinkedIn post adds an explicit framing qualifier, but the main article does not. Packaging notes must not upgrade edits that did not occur.
newsSourceFindings.evidence: Compare final news_report.md and publication_instructions.md section 3; exact byte bindings retained in newsroom-1-integrity-timeline-provenance.json.

newsSourceFindings.finding: The article’s prominent claim that no 2025–2026 independent comparison was located contradicts its own cited June 2026 higher-education study and the retained fetch. That study compares four tools on 160 known-ground-truth documents; its conclusions combine detector weaknesses with materially better Pangram performance. The article omits this countervailing result. Its advice against sole-evidence misconduct decisions remains supported, but broad failure claims must be narrowed.

The reporter also successfully fetched an August 2026 paper on editing and non-native writing but omitted it from the brief/article. Its abstract describes 135,389 paired documents and 13 detectors, finding heterogeneous responses to editing. This is relevant new evidence, not a missing-search gap.

The reviewer, article and release notes say arXiv:2306.04723 was not fetched, citing an unrelated recent log entry instead. The original run contains a successful fetch of the exact correct identifier and 5,263 retained characters. The abstract reports a proposed method’s stable cross-domain performance; framing this merely as support for universal robustness failure is one-sided.

The Liang result supports a 2023 sample-specific bias finding: seven detectors, 91 human TOEFL essays and 88 US eighth-grade essays, with 61.22% mean false-positive rate on the TOEFL sample. The manuscript’s more-than-half summary is broadly supported, but should state that it is a mean across those tools and cannot be transferred to every current detector. Pangram was not among the seven, so a later different model’s low-bias claim is not logically a direct contradiction.

The current X/LinkedIn posts attribute the historical finding, contrary to the reviewer’s criticism based on the old social file. Other posts still generalize all detectors and omit the version/sample caveat. Short posts require their own evidence-preserving check, not only consistency with a flawed parent article.

Both fact-checkers made zero web calls and zero reads of web-source snapshots. They read reporter briefs and manuscripts. Full source text remains in run records and same-agent snapshots, so not retained anywhere in this run is false; access/visibility for the reviewer is the narrower limitation. A recent-fetch list is not a complete provenance ledger, and missing from that list is not proof a source was not fetched. No reviewer source-fetch attempt or corresponding access-denial is recorded; this does not establish that the permission system made source verification impossible.

Both final article/social SHA pairs match the server’s current editorial review binding and the actual ZIP bytes. However, exact cited read evidence covers the revised main article but only the old social version, not the packaged social bytes. The N1 pass feedback also names old article IDs. A bundle-level hash binding must not be described as proof that every revised file was independently inspected.
